statement: Let $K \subseteq D$ be [division rings](c:division-ring) such that $xKx^{-1} \subseteq K$ for every nonzero $x \in D$. Then $K = D$, or every element of $K$ commutes with every element of $D$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a division subring of the [division ring](c:division-ring) $D$: it contains $1$ and is closed under subtraction, products and inverses of nonzero elements.
$K$ is a [normal subring](c:normal-subring) of $D$: $xKx^{-1} \subseteq K$ for every nonzero $x \in D$.

conclusion: Either $K = D$, or $K$ lies in the center of $D$.

proofs.name: Conjugates of a and of 1 + x
proofs.slogan: Compare the conjugates of $a \in K$ by $x$ and by $1 + x$ to show that $a$ commutes with every $x$ outside $K$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem: assume $K \ne D$ and prove that $K$ lies in the center. No assumption on the characteristic is needed.

roles.why: Closure under subtraction and inverses puts $(a_1 - a_2)^{-1}$ in $K$, and $1 \in K$ gives $1 + x \notin K$.
Conjugation of $a$ by $x$ and by $1 + x$ stays inside $K$.

steps.slogan: Fix $a \in K$ and $x \notin K$ and name the two conjugates of $a$.
steps.detail:
Since $K

e 0$, because $0$ and $1$ lie in $K$. By [normality](c:normal-subring), $a_1 = xax^{-1}$ and $a_2 = (1+x)a(1+x)^{-1}$ lie in $K$, so $xa = a_1x$ and $(1+x)a = a_2(1+x)$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two relations to get $(a_1 - a_2)x = a_2 - a$.
steps.detail: Expand $(1+x)a = a_2(1+x)$ to $a + xa = a_2 + a_2x$ and replace $xa$ by $a_1x$. This gives $a + a_1x = a_2 + a_2x$, so $(a_1 - a_2)x = a_2 - a$.

steps.slogan: Show that $a_1 = a_2$, because otherwise $x$ would lie in $K$.
steps.detail: If $a_1 \ne a_2$, then $a_1 - a_2$ is a nonzero element of $K$, so it has an inverse in $K$. Then $x = (a_1 - a_2)^{-1}(a_2 - a) \in K$, which is false. So $a_1 = a_2$, and the equation of step 2 gives $a_2 = a$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $a$ commutes with every element outside $K$.
steps.detail: From $a_1 = a$ we get $xax^{-1} = a$, so $xa = ax$. This holds for every $a \in K$ and every $x \in D \setminus K$.

steps.slogan: Extend the commutation to elements $y$ of $K$ by writing $y = (x + y) - x$.
steps.detail: Fix $x \in D \setminus K$ and $y \in K$. Then $x + y \notin K$, since $x = (x + y) - y$ would lie in $K$ otherwise. So $a$ commutes with $x + y$ and with $x$, hence with $y$. Thus $a$ commutes with all of $D$.

concepts.c:division-ring: Inverses of nonzero elements exist in $D$ and in $K$, which the proof uses twice.
concepts.c:normal-subring: Normality keeps the conjugates of $a$ inside $K$.

source.note: The textbook proof of the Cartan-Brauer-Hua theorem by comparing the conjugates by x and by 1 + x, as in Lam, A First Course in Noncommutative Rings, section 13.

statement: Let $b \ge 2$ be an integer and $p$ a [prime number](c:prime-number) with base-$b$ expansion $p = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b^k$, where $0 \le a_k \le b-1$ and $a_n \ne 0$. Then $f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k x^k$ is an [irreducible polynomial](c:irreducible-polynomial) in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

hypotheses.text: The integer $b \ge 2$ is the base, and the digits satisfy $0 \le a_k \le b - 1$ with $a_n \ne 0$.
The value $f(b) = p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).

conclusion: The polynomial $f$ is [irreducible](c:irreducible-polynomial) in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$: it is not a product of two non-constant integer polynomials.

proofs.name: Root region and prime value
proofs.slogan: Show that every root has real part below $b - 1/2$, so a factor with value $\pm 1$ at $b$ cannot exist.
proofs.scope: The case $n \ge 1$; for $n = 0$ the polynomial is the prime constant $p$. A constant factor is $\pm 1$, because it divides $a_n$ and $p$ while $0 < a_n < p$.

roles.why: The digit bounds drive the estimate on real parts and give $f(b-1) > 0$.
A prime value $p = g(b)h(b)$ forces one factor to equal $\pm 1$ at $b$.

steps.slogan: Split $f$ into non-constant factors and make one factor take the value $\pm 1$ at $b$.
steps.detail: Suppose $f = gh$ with $g, h \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ non-constant. Then $g(b)h(b) = f(b) = p$ is [prime](c:prime-number), so one factor, say $g$, has $|g(b)| = 1$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $w = 1/z$ for a root $z$ with real part at least $b - 1/2$.
steps.detail: Suppose $f(z) = 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} z \ge b - 1/2$; then $z \ne 0$. Write $w = 1/z = re^{i\theta}$. The condition on $z$ reads $r \le 2\cos\theta/(2b-1)$, so $|\theta| < \pi/2$ and $r \le q := 2/(2b-1)$. Dividing $f(z) = 0$ by $z^n$ gives $a_n + \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{n-k} w^k = 0$.

steps.slogan: Take real parts and separate the terms with a negative cosine.
steps.detail: The real part is $a_n + \sum_{k \ge 1} a_{n-k} r^k \cos k\theta$, with $a_n \ge 1$. A term with $\cos k\theta \ge 0$ is non-negative; any other term is at least $-(b-1)r^k$. So the real part is at least $1 - (b-1)\sum_{k \in N} r^k$, where $N = \{k \ge 1 : \cos k\theta < 0\}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the negative terms by a geometric series below $1/(b-1)$ and exclude such a root.
steps.detail: If $|\theta| \le \pi/4$, then $\cos\theta, \cos 2\theta \ge 0$, so $N \subseteq \{k \ge 3\}$ and $(b-1)\sum_{k\in N} r^k \le (b-1)q^3/(1-q) \le 8/9$. If $|\theta| > \pi/4$, then $N \subseteq \{k \ge 2\}$ and $r < \sqrt2/(2b-1)$, which gives at most $0.43$. The real part is positive, so $f(z) \ne 0$: every root has real part below $b - 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that every [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of $g$ lies closer to $b - 1$ than to $b$.
steps.detail: For $\operatorname{Re}\alpha < b - \tfrac12$ we have $|b-\alpha|^2 - |b-1-\alpha|^2 = 2(b - \tfrac12 - \operatorname{Re}\alpha) > 0$. Every root $\alpha$ of $g$ is a root of $f$, so $|b - \alpha| > |b - 1 - \alpha|$.

steps.slogan: Multiply over the roots of $g$ to get $|g(b)| > |g(b-1)| \ge 1$, a contradiction.
steps.detail: Write $g = c\prod_j (x - \alpha_j)$ with $c \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ and at least one root. Then $|g(b)| > |c|\prod_j |b-1-\alpha_j| = |g(b-1)|$. Now $f(b-1) \ge a_n(b-1)^n > 0$, so $g(b-1)$ is a nonzero integer and $|g(b-1)| \ge 1$. Hence $|g(b)| > 1$, which contradicts $|g(b)| = 1$.

concepts.c:prime-number: A prime value leaves no room for a factorization with both values large.
concepts.c:irreducible-polynomial: Irreducibility is what the contradiction proves.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The root region controls the distances $|b - \alpha|$ in the product.

source.note: The Polya-Szego root-region criterion with a direct estimate for every base b; the root estimate for all bases is due to Brillhart, Filaseta and Odlyzko, On an irreducibility theorem of A. Cohn, Canadian J. Math. 33 (1981), 1055-1059.

statement: Constructively, the category of [commutative C*-algebras](c:comm-c-star-algebra) with unit is dually equivalent to the category of compact completely regular [locales](c:locale): the Gelfand spectrum of $A$ is a locale and $A \to C(\operatorname{Spec} A)$ is an isomorphism. The proof is intuitionistic, so it holds in every [topos](c:topos) with a natural number object.

hypotheses.text: The ambient universe is a [topos](c:topos) with a natural number object, so only constructive logic is available.
The algebras are [commutative C*-algebras](c:comm-c-star-algebra) with unit, and the maps are unital $*$-homomorphisms.

conclusion: The functors $A \mapsto \operatorname{Spec} A$ and $X \mapsto C(X)$ form a dual equivalence between commutative unital C*-algebras and compact completely regular [locales](c:locale).

proofs.name: Spectrum locale and Stone-Weierstrass
proofs.slogan: Build the spectrum as a locale, the inverse functor as continuous functions on a locale, and show that both composites are isomorphic to the identity.
proofs.scope: The outline rests on the cited constructive proof; the steps name its real ingredients and the detail says what each does. Banaschewski and Mulvey proved the duality for Grothendieck toposes with Barr's theorem; the proof of Coquand and Spitters is fully constructive.

roles.why: Constructive logic is all that the proof may use, so it is valid inside the [topos](c:topos).
The Gelfand transform and the functor $C$ live on [commutative C*-algebras](c:comm-c-star-algebra) with unit.

steps.slogan: Define the spectrum of $A$ as a [locale](c:locale) given by generators and relations.
steps.detail: The generators stand for the open sets $\{a > 0\}$ for self-adjoint $a \in A$, and the relations encode the ordered ring structure of $A$. A presentation by generators and relations is a geometric construction, so it exists in any topos; its points are the characters of $A$ when the topos is classical, which recovers the classical Gelfand spectrum.

steps.slogan: Prove that the spectrum locale is compact and completely regular.
steps.detail: Compactness comes from the norm bound on $A$: the unit ball controls every cover. Complete regularity comes from the continuous functional calculus, which produces from each basic open set a function of $A$ that separates it. Both arguments avoid excluded middle.

steps.slogan: Define the inverse functor sending a compact completely regular [locale](c:locale) $X$ to the algebra $C(X)$.
steps.detail: The algebra $C(X)$ holds the locale maps from $X$ to the locale of complex numbers; compactness makes them bounded. The supremum norm and complex conjugation make $C(X)$ a commutative unital C*-algebra, and a locale map $X \to Y$ gives a $*$-homomorphism $C(Y) \to C(X)$ by composition.

steps.slogan: Show that the Gelfand transform $A \to C(\operatorname{Spec} A)$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: The transform is a $*$-homomorphism, and the C*-identity makes it isometric. Its image is dense by a constructive Stone-Weierstrass argument, and the image of a complete algebra under an isometry is closed. So the transform is onto, hence an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that $X \cong \operatorname{Spec} C(X)$ for every compact completely regular locale $X$.
steps.detail: Complete regularity says that the cozero sets of functions in $C(X)$ form a basis of $X$. So the opens of $X$ are recovered from the generators $\{f > 0\}$, and the unit map $X \to \operatorname{Spec} C(X)$ is an isomorphism of locales.

steps.slogan: Observe that every step is intuitionistic, so the duality holds inside any topos.
steps.detail: The two functors, their units and the isomorphism proofs use no excluded middle. Reading the proof in the internal logic of a [topos](c:topos) with a natural number object gives the duality there. The earlier proof of Banaschewski and Mulvey used Barr's theorem and covered Grothendieck toposes.

concepts.c:topos: The theorem is stated and proved inside the internal logic of a topos.
concepts.c:comm-c-star-algebra: These algebras are the objects on one side of the duality.
concepts.c:locale: Locales replace spaces, because the spectrum may lack points constructively.

source.ref: T. Coquand and B. Spitters, Constructive Gelfand duality for C*-algebras, Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 147 (2009), 323-337
source.note: A constructive proof of the duality; Banaschewski and Mulvey, A globalisation of the Gelfand duality theorem, Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 137 (2006), 62-103, give the version for Grothendieck toposes.

statement: Let a brick have sides $a_1 \mid a_2 \mid \dots \mid a_n$ (each divides the next): a [harmonic brick](c:harmonic-brick). If copies of it, with sides parallel to the axes, fill a [box](c:box) with sides $B_1, \dots, B_n$ without gaps or overlaps, then there are a permutation $\pi$ and integers $k_j \ge 1$ with $B_{\pi(j)} = k_j a_j$.

hypotheses.text: The brick is [harmonic](c:harmonic-brick): $a_{j+1}/a_j$ is a positive integer for every $j$.
Copies of the brick, with sides parallel to the axes, form a [packing](c:packing) of the [box](c:box) that leaves no gap and has no overlap.

conclusion: The box is a multiple of the brick: $B_{\pi(j)} = k_j a_j$ for a permutation $\pi$ and positive integers $k_j$.

proofs.name: Character integrals and Hall's theorem
proofs.slogan: Integrate a character over the box and over the bricks to count the box sides divisible by each $a_j$, then match sides with Hall's theorem.
proofs.scope: Real side lengths are allowed; $a \mid B$ means that $B/a$ is a positive integer. The proof first counts divisible sides and then builds the permutation.

roles.why: Divisibility of consecutive sides makes the $n - j + 1$ largest brick sides multiples of $a_j$.
The exact [packing](c:packing) turns the box integral into a sum of brick integrals.

steps.slogan: Choose $j$ coordinates and a character with period $a_j$ in exactly those coordinates.
steps.detail: Fix $j$ and a set $T$ of $j$ coordinates. Define $\chi(x) = \prod_{t \in T} e^{2\pi \mathrm{i}\, x_t / a_j}$, a function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that does not depend on the coordinates outside $T$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the integral of $\chi$ over any box as a product of one-dimensional integrals.
steps.detail: Over an interval of length $c$, the integral of $e^{2\pi \mathrm{i}\, x/a}$ is zero exactly when $a \mid c$, and the integral of the constant $1$ is $c \ne 0$. So $\int \chi$ over a box with sides $c_1, \dots, c_n$ vanishes exactly when $a_j \mid c_t$ for some $t \in T$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\chi$ has integral zero over every brick of the packing.
steps.detail: A placed brick has sides that rearrange $a_1, \dots, a_n$. The $n-j+1$ sides $a_j, \dots, a_n$ are multiples of $a_j$ because the chain divides. They sit in $n-j+1$ coordinates and $|T| = j$, so by pigeonhole some $t \in T$ carries a side divisible by $a_j$.

steps.slogan: Sum over the bricks to show that some $B_t$ with $t \in T$ is divisible by $a_j$.
steps.detail: The bricks cover the [box](c:box) and overlap only in sets of measure zero, so the integral of $\chi$ over the box is the sum of the brick integrals, which is $0$. By the product formula, $a_j \mid B_t$ for some $t \in T$.

steps.slogan: Count the box sides divisible by $a_j$: there are at least $n - j + 1$.
steps.detail: Every set $T$ of $j$ coordinates holds some $t$ with $a_j \mid B_t$. So at most $j - 1$ coordinates have $a_j \nmid B_t$, and at least $n - j + 1$ box sides are multiples of $a_j$. This holds for every $j = 1, \dots, n$.

steps.slogan: Match brick sides to box sides with Hall's theorem.
steps.detail: Join $a_j$ to the box side $B_t$ when $a_j \mid B_t$. The chain makes these neighbor sets nested, so a set $S$ of brick sides has exactly the neighbors of $a_{\min S}$, at least $n - \min S + 1 \ge |S|$ of them. Hall's theorem gives a perfect matching $\pi$, so $B_{\pi(j)} = k_j a_j$ with $k_j$ a positive integer.

concepts.c:harmonic-brick: The divisibility chain is what makes every brick integral vanish.
concepts.c:packing: A packing without gaps lets the box integral split over the bricks.
concepts.c:box: The box sides $B_t$ are the numbers whose divisibility the proof counts.

source.note: A weights argument in the style of N. G. de Bruijn, Filling boxes with bricks, American Mathematical Monthly 76 (1969), 37-40, with Hall's marriage theorem for the final matching.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [compact Riemann surfaces](c:compact-riemann-surface), and let $Y$ have [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) at least $2$. Then there are only finitely many non-constant holomorphic maps $X \to Y$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ and $Y$ are [compact Riemann surfaces](c:compact-riemann-surface).
The [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) of $Y$ is at least $2$.

conclusion: The set of non-constant holomorphic maps $X \to Y$ is finite.

proofs.name: Jacobian lattice argument
proofs.slogan: Bound the degree, pull back to Jacobians, count the bounded points of a lattice, and show that the pullback determines the map.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for non-constant maps; if $g_X < g_Y$ there are none. The outline follows the Jacobian argument of Martens, and each step names the published ingredient.

roles.why: Compactness gives Jacobians, the pullback of divisors and the degree of a map.
Genus at least $2$ makes the degree bound finite and rules out translations of the curve $Y$.

steps.slogan: Bound the degree of every non-constant map by the Riemann-Hurwitz formula.
steps.detail: A non-constant $f\colon X \to Y$ has a degree $d \ge 1$ and satisfies $2g_X - 2 \ge d\,(2g_Y - 2)$ by the Riemann-Hurwitz formula. Since $g_Y \ge 2$, we get $d \le D := (2g_X - 2)/(2g_Y - 2)$, a bound that does not depend on $f$.

steps.slogan: Attach to $f$ the pullback homomorphism $f^*\colon J(Y) \to J(X)$ of [Jacobians](c:jacobian-variety).
steps.detail: Pulling back divisors gives a homomorphism $f^*$ of Jacobian varieties. Its transpose for the canonical principal polarizations is the pushforward $f_*$, and $f_*f^* = d$ on $J(Y)$.

steps.slogan: Show that only finitely many homomorphisms $f^*$ can occur.
steps.detail: The group $\operatorname{Hom}(J(Y), J(X))$ is free abelian of finite rank, and $\varphi \mapsto \operatorname{tr}(\varphi'\varphi)$, the trace of the analytic representation, is a positive definite quadratic form on it. For $\varphi = f^*$ the value is $d\,g_Y \le D g_Y$. A lattice has finitely many points in a ball, so $f^*$ takes finitely many values.

steps.slogan: Show that $f^*$ determines the map $f$.
steps.detail: If $f^* = h^*$, then $f_* = h_*$, so $f - h$ is a constant $c$ on the curve $Y \subset J(Y)$ and $Y + c = Y$. Translation by $c$ gives an [automorphism](c:automorphism-group) of $Y$, of finite order by Hurwitz's bound, that acts trivially on holomorphic differentials. With $g_Y \ge 2$ Riemann-Hurwitz forces it to be the identity, so $c = 0$ and $f = h$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two finiteness statements to bound the number of maps.
steps.detail: By steps 1 to 3 only finitely many homomorphisms occur as $f^*$ for non-constant $f$. By step 4 each of them comes from at most one map. So the set of non-constant maps is finite.

concepts.c:compact-riemann-surface: Compactness gives Jacobians and finite-degree covers.
concepts.c:genus-of-a-surface: The genus decides the sign in the Riemann-Hurwitz bound.
concepts.c:jacobian-variety: The Jacobians carry the lattice of homomorphisms that is counted.
concepts.c:automorphism-group: The finite automorphism group of $Y$ rules out nonzero translations.

source.ref: H. H. Martens, Observations on morphisms of closed Riemann surfaces, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 10 (1978), 209-212
source.note: The Jacobian proof that a map into a curve of genus at least 2 is determined by its action on homology; Kani, Inventiones Mathematicae 85 (1986), gives effective bounds.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a square of side $a$. A horizontal line moves uniformly from $DC$ to $AB$ while a ray from $A$ turns uniformly from $AD$ to $AB$ in the same time. Their crossing point traces the [quadratrix](c:quadratrix) and has a [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $G$ on $AB$ with $AG = 2a/\pi$, so $AG : AB = AB : \operatorname{arc} BD$.

hypotheses.text: $ABCD$ is a square of side $a$ with $A = (0,0)$, $B = (a,0)$, $C = (a,a)$ and $D = (0,a)$.
At time $t \in [0,1)$ the line is $y = a(1-t)$ and the ray from $A$ makes the angle $\tfrac{\pi}{2}(1-t)$ with $AB$; the [quadratrix](c:quadratrix) is the path of their crossing point $P(t)$.

conclusion: The point $P(t)$ has the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $G = (2a/\pi, 0)$ as $t \to 1$, so $AG = 2a/\pi$ and $AG \cdot \operatorname{arc} BD = AB^2$.

proofs.name: Angle parametrization and a limit
proofs.slogan: Write the crossing point in the angle $\theta$ and take the limit of $\theta/\tan\theta$ as $\theta \to 0$.
proofs.scope: The crossing point exists for $t < 1$, since the two lines coincide at $t = 1$, so the end point is a limit. The proof computes this limit and the ratio with the arc.

roles.why: The side $a$ sets the scale, and the coordinates make the ray and the line explicit.
Uniform motion ties the height of the line to the angle of the ray by $y = 2a\theta/\pi$.

steps.slogan: Parametrize both motions by the angle $\theta$ of the ray.
steps.detail: Put $\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{2}(1-t) \in (0, \pi/2]$. The ray is $y = x\tan\theta$, and the horizontal line is $y = a(1-t) = 2a\theta/\pi$.

steps.slogan: Solve for the crossing point $P$ of the ray and the line.
steps.detail: Setting $x\tan\theta = 2a\theta/\pi$ gives $P = \bigl(\tfrac{2a}{\pi}\cdot\tfrac{\theta}{\tan\theta},\ \tfrac{2a\theta}{\pi}\bigr)$ for $0 < \theta < \pi/2$. At $\theta = \pi/2$ the crossing point is $D$.

steps.slogan: Take the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) of $P$ as $\theta \to 0$.
steps.detail: Since $\sin\theta/\theta \to 1$ and $\cos\theta \to 1$, we get $\theta/\tan\theta = (\theta/\sin\theta)\cos\theta \to 1$. Also $2a\theta/\pi \to 0$. Hence $P \to G = (2a/\pi, 0)$, a point of $AB$ with $AG = 2a/\pi$.

steps.slogan: Compare $AG$ with the length of the arc $BD$.
steps.detail: The arc $BD$ of the circle with center $A$ and radius $a$ has length $\pi a/2$. So $AG \cdot \operatorname{arc} BD = \tfrac{2a}{\pi}\cdot\tfrac{\pi a}{2} = a^2 = AB^2$, which is the proportion $AG : AB = AB : \operatorname{arc} BD$.

concepts.c:quadratrix: The curve is the path of the crossing point of the two motions.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: The end point $G$ is a limit, not a value, of the curve.

source.note: The classical argument of Dinostratus in modern coordinates; the quadratrix of Hippias is described in Heath, A History of Greek Mathematics, volume 1.

statement: Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a [sigma-finite measure](c:sigma-finite-measure) space, and let $T\colon L^1 \to L^1$ be linear and a [contraction](c:l1-contraction) of the $L^1$ norm that also contracts the $L^\infty$ norm on $L^1 \cap L^\infty$. Then for every $f \in L^1$ the averages $\frac1N\sum_{n<N}T^nf$ converge [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere).

hypotheses.text: $(\Omega,\mu)$ is a [sigma-finite measure](c:sigma-finite-measure) space.
$T\colon L^1 \to L^1$ is linear with $\|Tf\|_1 \le \|f\|_1$, a [contraction](c:l1-contraction) of $L^1$.
$\|Tf\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty$ for every $f \in L^1 \cap L^\infty$.

conclusion: For every $f \in L^1$, the limit of $\frac1N\sum_{n<N}T^nf$ exists [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere).

proofs.name: Maximal inequality and a dense set
proofs.slogan: Prove a weak type maximal inequality for the averages, show convergence on a dense set of fixed vectors and coboundaries, then extend by density.
proofs.scope: The case $f \in L^1$; the same density argument with the $L^p$ maximal inequality gives $L^p$ for $1 < p < \infty$. The outline follows the route of Hopf and of Dunford and Schwartz.

roles.why: Sets of finite [measure](c:sigma-finite-measure) exhaust $\Omega$, which Hopf's argument needs.
The $L^1$ [contraction](c:l1-contraction) gives Hopf's lemma and the weak type $(1,1)$ bound.
The $L^\infty$ bound gives $S1 \le 1$, and with $L^1$ it gives the $L^2$ contraction.

steps.slogan: Replace $T$ by its positive modulus $|T|$, which keeps both contraction properties.
steps.detail: The modulus $|T|$ is the smallest positive operator with $|Tf| \le |T||f|$. On $L^1$ it exists and again contracts $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ (Chacon and Krengel). With $A_N = \frac1N\sum_{n<N}T^n$ we get $|A_Nf| \le A_N^{|T|}|f|$ pointwise, so a maximal inequality for positive operators controls $\sup_N|A_Nf|$.

steps.slogan: Prove the weak type $(1,1)$ maximal inequality from Hopf's maximal ergodic lemma.
steps.detail: For a positive $S$ with $\|S\|_1 \le 1$ and $S1 \le 1$, Hopf's lemma gives $\int_{\{\sup_n S_nf > 0\}} f\,d\mu \ge 0$, where $S_n = \sum_{k<n}S^k$. Applied to $f - \lambda\mathbf 1_F$ with $\mu(F) < \infty$, it gives $\mu\{\sup_N A_Nf > \lambda\} \le \|f\|_1/\lambda$ for $f \ge 0$. By step 1, $\mu\{\sup_N|A_Nf| > \lambda\} \le \|f\|_1/\lambda$ for all $f$.

steps.slogan: Split $L^2$ into the fixed vectors of $T$ and the closure of the coboundaries.
steps.detail: By Riesz-Thorin, $T$ contracts every $L^p$, in particular $L^2$. The mean ergodic theorem for a contraction of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) gives $L^2 = \operatorname{Fix}(T) \oplus \overline{(I-T)L^2}$, with $A_Nf$ converging in $L^2$.

steps.slogan: Show convergence almost everywhere on fixed vectors and on coboundaries.
steps.detail: If $Tg_0 = g_0$, the averages equal $g_0$. For a coboundary, $A_N(g - Tg) = (g - T^Ng)/N$ and $\sum_N\|T^Ng/N\|_2^2 \le \|g\|_2^2\sum N^{-2} < \infty$, so $T^Ng/N \to 0$ almost everywhere. The span $V$ of both kinds is dense in $L^2$ by step 3.

steps.slogan: Extend convergence almost everywhere from $V$ to all of $L^2$.
steps.detail: The operator $Mf = \sup_N|A_Nf|$ is sublinear, of weak type $(1,1)$ and bounded on $L^\infty$, so Marcinkiewicz interpolation gives $\|Mf\|_2 \le C\|f\|_2$. The oscillation of $A_Nf$ is at most $2M(f - v)$ for $v \in V$. Taking $v_k \to f$ in $L^2$ shows that the oscillation vanishes almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Extend to $L^1$ by density of $L^1 \cap L^2$ and the weak type $(1,1)$ bound.
steps.detail: Integrable simple functions $g_k$ lie in $L^1 \cap L^2$ and converge to $f$ in $L^1$. The oscillation of $A_Nf$ is at most $2M(f - g_k)$ almost everywhere, because $A_Ng_k$ converges almost everywhere. By step 2, $\mu\{2M(f-g_k) > 2\delta\} \le \|f - g_k\|_1/\delta \to 0$, so the oscillation is zero almost everywhere.

concepts.c:sigma-finite-measure: Sets of finite measure that exhaust the space make Hopf's lemma usable.
concepts.c:l1-contraction: The $L^1$ contraction property is the input of Hopf's maximal lemma.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: Convergence holds outside a set of measure zero, not everywhere.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The mean ergodic theorem for the $L^2$ contraction is a Hilbert space statement.

source.ref: N. Dunford and J. T. Schwartz, Convergence almost everywhere of operator averages, Journal of Rational Mechanics and Analysis 5 (1956), 129-178
source.note: The original proof; the same ingredients (a maximal inequality and convergence on a dense set) appear in U. Krengel, Ergodic Theorems, de Gruyter 1985, chapter 2.

statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be [von Neumann algebras](c:von-neumann-algebra), neither isomorphic to $\mathbb C \oplus \mathbb C$ and neither with a type $I_2$ summand. Every order isomorphism $f$ between their [posets of commutative subalgebras](c:poset-of-commutative-subalgebras) $\mathcal V(M)$ and $\mathcal V(N)$ is induced by a unique [Jordan](c:jordan-algebra) $*$-isomorphism $g\colon M \to N$: $g[S] = f(S)$ for all $S$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ and $N$ are [von Neumann algebras](c:von-neumann-algebra), in particular [C*-algebras](c:c-star-algebra).
Neither algebra has a direct summand of type $I_2$, and neither is isomorphic to $\mathbb C \oplus \mathbb C$.
The map $f\colon \mathcal V(M) \to \mathcal V(N)$ is an order isomorphism of the [posets of commutative subalgebras](c:poset-of-commutative-subalgebras), that is, of abelian von Neumann subalgebras.

conclusion: There is exactly one [Jordan](c:jordan-algebra) $*$-isomorphism $g\colon M \to N$ with $g[S] = f(S)$ for every abelian von Neumann subalgebra $S$ of $M$.

proofs.name: Boolean subalgebras and Dye's theorem
proofs.slogan: Read the order isomorphism as an orthoisomorphism of projection lattices, extend it to a Jordan isomorphism by Dye's theorem, and show uniqueness.
proofs.scope: The theorem of Doering and Harding for von Neumann algebras; Hamhalter extended it to more general C*-algebras. The outline names the ingredients of the cited proof and does not reprove them.

roles.why: A [von Neumann algebra](c:von-neumann-algebra) is spanned by its projections, so its abelian subalgebras match Boolean subalgebras of $P(M)$.
The exclusions let the lifting step work, make Dye's theorem apply and force uniqueness.
The order isomorphism $f$ is the input from which the orthoisomorphism is built.

steps.slogan: Identify the poset of abelian subalgebras with the complete Boolean subalgebras of the projection lattice.
steps.detail: An abelian von Neumann subalgebra $S$ is generated by its projections, and $P(S)$ is a complete Boolean subalgebra of the orthomodular lattice $P(M)$. Conversely, every complete Boolean subalgebra generates an abelian von Neumann algebra. So $f$ becomes an order isomorphism of the posets of complete Boolean subalgebras of $P(M)$ and $P(N)$.

steps.slogan: Lift the order isomorphism to an orthoisomorphism of the projection lattices.
steps.detail: The atoms of $\mathcal V(M)$ above $\mathbb C1$ are the algebras $\mathbb C1 + \mathbb Cp$ with $p \ne 0, 1$, so $f$ matches the pairs $\{p, 1-p\}$. The cited paper shows that, under the exclusions of the theorem, the order structure also fixes which member of each pair goes where. This gives an orthoisomorphism $\varphi\colon P(M) \to P(N)$ with $f(S)$ generated by $\varphi[P(S)]$.

steps.slogan: Extend the orthoisomorphism to a Jordan $*$-isomorphism with Dye's theorem.
steps.detail: Dye's theorem says that an orthoisomorphism between the projection lattices of von Neumann algebras without a type $I_2$ summand is the restriction of a Jordan $*$-isomorphism $g\colon M \to N$. A von Neumann algebra is the norm closed span of its projections, so $\varphi$ determines $g$.

steps.slogan: Check that $g$ sends every abelian subalgebra $S$ onto $f(S)$.
steps.detail: Each $S \in \mathcal V(M)$ is generated by $P(S)$. The map $g$ equals $\varphi$ on $P(S)$, and $f(S)$ is generated by $\varphi[P(S)]$, so $g[S] = f(S)$. This proves existence.

steps.slogan: Show that two such Jordan isomorphisms coincide, which gives uniqueness.
steps.detail: If $g$ and $g'$ both satisfy $g[S] = f(S)$, then $\theta = g'^{-1}g$ is a Jordan automorphism of $M$ that maps every abelian subalgebra onto itself. So $\theta(p) \in \{p, 1-p\}$ for every projection $p$. The cited paper shows that the exclusions force $\theta = \mathrm{id}$.

concepts.c:von-neumann-algebra: Projections span the algebra, so projection data determine the whole algebra.
concepts.c:c-star-algebra: The theorem is the von Neumann case of a result for C*-algebras.
concepts.c:poset-of-commutative-subalgebras: This poset is the only input; it encodes the Boolean subalgebras.
concepts.c:jordan-algebra: The recovered structure is the Jordan product, not the associative product.

source.ref: A. Doering and J. Harding, Abelian subalgebras and the Jordan structure of a von Neumann algebra, Houston Journal of Mathematics 42 (2016); arXiv:1009.4945
source.note: The proof combines the order structure of Boolean subalgebras with H. A. Dye, On the geometry of projections in certain operator algebras, Annals of Mathematics 61 (1955), 73-89.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $(X, Y)$ a matching pair of $G$-spaces. Two $G$-maps $f, g\colon X \to Y$ are $G$-homotopic if and only if $\deg f^H = \deg g^H$ for every isotropy group $H$ of $X$. So the [degrees](c:degree-of-a-map) determine the class of $f$ in the [equivariant cohomotopy](c:equivariant-cohomotopy) set.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $X$ is a finite-dimensional $G$-CW complex.

For each isotropy group $H$ of $X$, with $n_H = \dim X^H$: $H^{n_H}(X^H;\mathbb Z) \cong \mathbb Z$, the [fixed-point space](c:fixed-point-space-2) $Y^H$ is $(n_H-1)$-connected with $\pi_{n_H}(Y^H) \cong \mathbb Z$, and the Weyl group acts on the orientations of $X^H$ and $Y^H$ alike.

conclusion: The maps $f$ and $g$ are $G$-homotopic exactly when their [degrees](c:degree-of-a-map) agree, $\deg f^H = \deg g^H$, for all isotropy groups $H$ of $X$.

proofs.name: Induction over isotropy and obstruction theory
proofs.slogan: Deform one map stratum by stratum from the largest isotropy to the smallest, where the only obstruction is the difference of degrees.
proofs.scope: The injectivity of the degree map on equivariant homotopy classes; the description of its image by congruences is not proved here. The outline follows the equivariant Hopf theorem of tom Dieck.

roles.why: A [finite group](c:finite-group) has finitely many isotropy groups and finite Weyl groups, so the induction ends.
The matching conditions leave one obstruction group for each isotropy group, a copy of $\mathbb Z$ detected by degrees.

steps.slogan: Order the isotropy groups and treat the larger isotropy groups first.
steps.detail: For an isotropy group $H$, let $X^{>H} \subseteq X^H$ be the points whose isotropy is strictly larger than $H$. A $G$-map on the part of $X$ with isotropy $H$ is a $W_GH$-map on $X^H$ that is already given on $X^{>H}$, and $W_GH$ acts freely on $X^H \setminus X^{>H}$.

steps.slogan: Make $f$ and $g$ agree on the part with larger isotropy by equivariant homotopy extension.
steps.detail: By induction, $f$ and $g$ are homotopic on $X^{>H}$. The homotopy extension property of the $G$-CW pair lets us deform $g$ so that $f = g$ on all points with isotropy strictly larger than $H$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the remaining problem to a single obstruction class.
steps.detail: The maps $f^H$ and $g^H$ differ on free $W_GH$-cells of dimension at most $n_H$. Since $Y^H$ is $(n_H-1)$-connected, every obstruction to a homotopy rel $X^{>H}$ vanishes except one class in $H^{n_H}_{W_GH}(X^H, X^{>H}; \pi_{n_H}Y^H)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the obstruction class with the difference of the $H$-degrees.
steps.detail: The matching conditions make this group a copy of $\mathbb Z$ with compatible orientations, and the class of the pair $(f, g)$ is detected by $\deg f^H - \deg g^H$. For the trivial group this is the Hopf degree theorem. So equal degrees make the class zero.

steps.slogan: Conclude the $G$-homotopy by induction over all isotropy groups.
steps.detail: If all degrees agree, the obstruction vanishes at every stage, so homotopies rel the larger isotropy strata exist and glue to a $G$-homotopy $f \simeq_G g$. Conversely, a $G$-homotopy restricts to homotopies of $f^H$ and $g^H$, and homotopic maps have equal degree.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness of $G$ makes the induction over isotropy groups terminate.
concepts.c:fixed-point-space-2: Each fixed-point space $X^H$ and $Y^H$ carries one degree.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-map: Degrees on the fixed-point spaces are the complete invariant.
concepts.c:equivariant-cohomotopy: The set of equivariant homotopy classes is the equivariant cohomotopy set that the degrees classify.

source.ref: T. tom Dieck, Transformation Groups and Representation Theory, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 766, Springer 1979, section 8.4
source.note: The equivariant Hopf theorem, in the form for matching pairs of G-spaces used in equivariant cohomotopy by Sati and Schreiber, arXiv:1909.12277.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $X$ a $G$-[simplicial set](c:simplicial-set). For every subgroup $H$, the integration map $\int\colon A_{PL}(X^H) \to C^*(X^H;\mathbb Q)$ is a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism), natural in the orbit $G/H$. So the diagram $G/H \mapsto A_{PL}(X^H)$ computes the rational [equivariant cohomology](c:equivariant-cohomology) $G/H \mapsto H^*(X^H;\mathbb Q)$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
$X$ is a $G$-[simplicial set](c:simplicial-set), so each fixed set $X^H$ is a simplicial subset.

conclusion: Integration is a natural [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) of diagrams over the orbit category, so $H^*(A_{PL}(X^H)) \cong H^*(X^H;\mathbb Q)$ naturally in $G/H$.

proofs.name: Reduction to the plain theorem on fixed sets
proofs.slogan: Apply the plain PL de Rham theorem to every fixed point set and check that integration is natural over the orbit category.
proofs.scope: The comparison of the PL de Rham diagram with rational cochains; the minimal model consequences in Triantafillou's paper are not proved here. The proof works fixed point set by fixed point set.

roles.why: The argument treats each subgroup separately and never uses finiteness; finiteness only keeps the orbit category small.
A $G$-[simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) has fixed sets that are simplicial sets, so the plain theorem applies to each.

steps.slogan: Take fixed point sets as simplicial subsets and check that they form a diagram over orbits.
steps.detail: For a subgroup $H$, $X^H$ is the simplicial subset of simplices fixed by $H$. A $G$-map $G/K \to G/H$ is given by $eK \mapsto aH$ with $a^{-1}Ka \subseteq H$, and it induces $X^H \to X^K$, $x \mapsto ax$. So $G/H \mapsto X^H$ is a contravariant functor on the orbit category.

steps.slogan: Apply the plain PL de Rham theorem to each simplicial set $X^H$.
steps.detail: For every simplicial set $K$ the integration map $\int_K\colon A_{PL}(K) \to C^*(K;\mathbb Q)$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Taking $K = X^H$ gives a quasi-isomorphism for every subgroup $H$.

steps.slogan: Check that integration commutes with the maps induced by orbit morphisms.
steps.detail: Integration is a natural transformation between functors on simplicial sets. An orbit morphism $G/K \to G/H$ induces a simplicial map $X^H \to X^K$, so the square formed by $A_{PL}$ and $C^*$ over it commutes. Hence $\int$ is a morphism of diagrams over the orbit category.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the diagram map is an objectwise quasi-isomorphism and compare the cohomology diagrams.
steps.detail: A morphism of diagrams that is a [quasi-isomorphism](c:quasi-isomorphism) at every object induces isomorphisms in cohomology at every object, and these are natural because the morphism is. So $H^*(A_{PL}(X^H)) \cong H^*(X^H;\mathbb Q)$ naturally in $G/H$, the rational [equivariant cohomology](c:equivariant-cohomology) of $X$.

concepts.c:finite-group: The group acts, and its subgroups index the fixed point sets.
concepts.c:simplicial-set: Fixed points of a simplicial $G$-set are simplicial subsets.
concepts.c:quasi-isomorphism: Quasi-isomorphisms identify the cohomology of the two cochain models.
concepts.c:equivariant-cohomology: The diagram of fixed set cohomologies is the rational equivariant cohomology.

source.note: Reduction to the plain PL de Rham theorem (Sullivan; Bousfield and Gugenheim) in the setting of D. Triantafillou, Equivariant minimal models, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 274 (1982), 509-532.

statement: Let $G \subset \mathbb C$ be a [Carathéodory domain](c:caratheodory-domain), for example the interior of a Jordan curve. Every [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on $G$ with $\int_G |f|^2\,dA < \infty$ is the limit in $L^2(G)$ of [polynomials](c:polynomial-approximation). That is, polynomials are dense in the Bergman space $A^2(G)$.

hypotheses.text: $G \subset \mathbb C$ is a [Carathéodory domain](c:caratheodory-domain): a bounded simply connected domain, such as the interior of a Jordan curve.
$f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $G$ and square integrable, $\int_G |f|^2\,dA < \infty$.

proofs.name: Conformal transplant to outer domains
proofs.slogan: Transplant $f$ to a slightly larger domain by a conformal map, approximate there by polynomials with Runge's theorem, and let the larger domain shrink to $G$.
proofs.scope: The Hilbert space case $A^2(G)$, which is the original form of the theorem; the extension to $A^p$ is a separate statement. The kernel property of a Carathéodory domain is the one place where the shape of $G$ enters.

roles.why: The [Carathéodory](c:caratheodory-domain) property makes the outer domains shrink to $G$, so the transplanted functions converge to $f$.
Holomorphy and square integrability make the transplant holomorphic with the same norm as $f$.

steps.slogan: Build simply connected outer domains $G_\rho$ that contain $\overline G$ and shrink to $G$.
steps.detail: Let $\Omega$ be the unbounded component of $\hat{\mathbb C} \setminus \overline G$ and $\Phi\colon \Omega \to \{|w| > 1\}$ a Riemann map with $\Phi(\infty) = \infty$. For $\rho > 1$ put $G_\rho = \hat{\mathbb C} \setminus \Phi^{-1}(\{|w| \ge \rho\})$, a bounded simply connected domain containing $K = \hat{\mathbb C} \setminus \Omega \supseteq \overline G$. For a Carathéodory domain, the kernel of the $G_\rho$ as $\rho \downarrow 1$ is $G$.

steps.slogan: Map $G$ onto each $G_\rho$ by a Riemann map, and let these maps converge to the identity.
steps.detail: Fix $z_0 \in G$. Let $\psi_\rho\colon G \to G_\rho$ be the Riemann map with $\psi_\rho(z_0) = z_0$ and $\psi_\rho'(z_0) > 0$. By Carathéodory's kernel theorem, $\psi_\rho^{-1} \to \mathrm{id}$ locally uniformly on $G$ as $\rho \downarrow 1$, and so do the derivatives.

steps.slogan: Transplant $f$ to $G_\rho$ with the weight $(\psi_\rho^{-1})'$.
steps.detail: Put $H_\rho = (f \circ \psi_\rho^{-1})\,(\psi_\rho^{-1})'$ on $G_\rho$. It is holomorphic. Because $|(\psi_\rho^{-1})'|^2$ is the Jacobian of $\psi_\rho^{-1}$, the change of variables gives $\|H_\rho\|_{A^2(G_\rho)} = \|f\|_{A^2(G)}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $H_\rho \to f$ in $A^2(G)$ as $\rho \downarrow 1$.
steps.detail: On compact subsets of $G$, $H_\rho \to f$ uniformly by step 2, so $H_\rho \to f$ weakly in $A^2(G)$. The same change of variables gives $\int_G |H_\rho|^2 = \int_{\psi_\rho^{-1}(G)} |f|^2 \to \|f\|^2$, because the sets $\psi_\rho^{-1}(G) \subseteq G$ exhaust $G$. Weak convergence with convergence of norms gives convergence in norm.

steps.slogan: Approximate $H_\rho$ uniformly on $\overline G$ by polynomials with Runge's theorem.
steps.detail: The set $K = \hat{\mathbb C} \setminus \Omega$ is compact, contains $\overline G$, lies in $G_\rho$ and has connected complement $\Omega$. Since $H_\rho$ is holomorphic on $G_\rho \supset K$, Runge's theorem gives polynomials converging to $H_\rho$ uniformly on $K$. Hence they converge in $A^2(G)$, because $G$ has finite area.

steps.slogan: Combine the two approximations to approximate $f$ itself.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $\rho$ with $\|f - H_\rho\|_{A^2(G)} < \varepsilon/2$, then a polynomial $p$ with $\|H_\rho - p\|_{A^2(G)} < \varepsilon/2$. Then $\|f - p\|_{A^2(G)} < \varepsilon$, so the polynomials are dense in $A^2(G)$.

concepts.c:caratheodory-domain: The kernel property lets the outer domains shrink to $G$.
concepts.c:polynomial-approximation: Polynomials are the approximants; Runge's theorem supplies them on the outer domain.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy makes the transplanted function holomorphic on the larger domain.

source.note: The conformal mapping argument of O. J. Farrell, On approximation to an analytic function by polynomials, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 40 (1934), 908-914, and of Markushevich, written in the Hilbert space form.

statement: In a non-equilateral triangle, the [nine-point circle](c:nine-point-circle) is internally tangent to the [incircle](c:incircle) and externally tangent to each of the three [excircles](c:excircle).

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a nondegenerate triangle with side lengths $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, circumradius $R$ and inradius $r$.
The triangle is not equilateral.

conclusion: The incircle touches the nine-point circle from inside, and each excircle touches it from outside.

proofs.name: Distance of the centers by vectors
proofs.slogan: Compute the squared distance from the nine-point center to the incenter and to each excenter, and compare it with the radii.
proofs.scope: The incircle and the excircle opposite $A$; the other two excircles follow by relabeling. A non-equilateral triangle has $R > 2r$, so the two circles are distinct.

roles.why: The side lengths give the dot products and the weights of the incenter and excenters.
Non-equilateral gives $R > 2r$, so the distance of the centers is a positive difference of radii.

steps.slogan: Place the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) at the origin and write the centers as weighted averages.
steps.detail: Let $O = 0$, so $|A| = |B| = |C| = R$, $A\cdot B = R^2 - \gamma^2/2$, $A\cdot C = R^2 - \beta^2/2$ and $B\cdot C = R^2 - \alpha^2/2$. The nine-point circle has center $N = (A+B+C)/2$ and radius $R/2$. The incenter is $I = (\alpha A + \beta B + \gamma C)/(2s)$, where $2s = \alpha + \beta + \gamma$.

steps.slogan: Expand $|I|^2$, $N\cdot I$ and $|N|^2$ with the dot products.
steps.detail: Expanding gives $|I|^2 = R^2 - \alpha\beta\gamma/(2s)$, $N \cdot I = \tfrac32 R^2 - S/(8s)$ and $|N|^2 = (9R^2 - \alpha^2 - \beta^2 - \gamma^2)/4$. Here $S = \alpha(\beta^2+\gamma^2) + \beta(\gamma^2+\alpha^2) + \gamma(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the symmetric sums with $s$, $r$ and $R$.
steps.detail: Let $q = \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha$. The area $K = rs = \alpha\beta\gamma/(4R)$ gives $\alpha\beta\gamma = 4Rrs$, and Heron's formula gives $q = s^2 + r^2 + 4Rr$. Also $S = 2sq - 3\alpha\beta\gamma$ and $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2 = 4s^2 - 2q$.

steps.slogan: Combine the terms to get $|N - I|^2 = (R/2 - r)^2$.
steps.detail: We have $|N-I|^2 = |N|^2 - 2N\cdot I + |I|^2 = \tfrac{R^2}{4} - 2Rr - \tfrac{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2}{4} + \tfrac{S}{4s}$. By step 3 the last two terms sum to $q - s^2 - 3Rr = r^2 + Rr$. So $|N-I|^2 = \tfrac{R^2}{4} - Rr + r^2$.

steps.slogan: Read the tangency of the incircle from the distance and the radii.
steps.detail: The incircle has radius $r$ and the nine-point circle has radius $R/2$. Euler's relation $OI^2 = R^2 - 2Rr$ gives $R \ge 2r$, with equality only if $I = O$, that is for the equilateral triangle. So $R/2 > r$ here, the distance of the centers $R/2 - r$ is the difference of the radii, and the circles touch from inside.

steps.slogan: Repeat the computation with the weights $(-\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ for the excircle opposite $A$.
steps.detail: The excenter is $I_a = (-\alpha A + \beta B + \gamma C)/(2(s-\alpha))$ and $r_a = K/(s-\alpha)$. The same expansion gives $|N - I_a|^2 = (R/2 + r_a)^2$, the square of the sum of the radii, so the circles touch from outside. Relabeling gives the other two excircles.

concepts.c:circumcenter: The circumcenter is the origin, which makes the dot products simple.
concepts.c:nine-point-circle: Its center $N$ and radius $R/2$ are the data that the distances compare.
concepts.c:incircle: Its center and radius $r$ give the internal tangency.
concepts.c:excircle: Their centers and radii give the external tangencies.

source.note: A vector proof of Feuerbach's theorem; Coxeter and Greitzer, Geometry Revisited, chapter 5, give an inversion proof.

statement: Let $\mathcal P$ be a twisted [modular operad](c:modular-operad) of chain complexes. The Feynman transform $F\mathcal P$ is a [graph complex](c:graph-complex): the sum over stable graphs of dual vertex labels, with differential $d = d_{\mathcal P} + d_{\mathrm{split}}$. Then $d^2 = 0$, $F\mathcal P$ is a twisted modular operad, and its genus-$0$ part is the shifted [cobar construction](c:bar-construction) of the underlying cyclic operad.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal P$ is a twisted [modular operad](c:modular-operad) in chain complexes over a field of characteristic zero.
The graphs are stable: a vertex of genus $g_v$ with $n_v$ half-edges has $2g_v - 2 + n_v > 0$.

conclusion: The differential $d$ squares to zero, $F\mathcal P$ is a twisted modular operad, and in genus $0$ it is the shifted [cobar construction](c:bar-construction) of the cyclic operad of $\mathcal P$.

proofs.name: Graph sum and sign cancellation
proofs.slogan: Sum the dual vertex labels over stable graphs, split vertices along new edges, and check that signs cancel in $d^2$.
proofs.scope: The construction and its stated properties for a twisted dg modular operad; the equivalence $FF\mathcal P \simeq \mathcal P$ is a separate theorem. The outline follows the definition and first properties in the cited paper.

roles.why: The composition maps of $\mathcal P$ give the vertex-splitting differential and the gluing structure.
Stability keeps the set of graphs of each type finite, so the graph sum is a finite sum.

steps.slogan: Define $F\mathcal P(g,n)$ as a sum over stable graphs of type $(g,n)$.
steps.detail: For each stable graph $\Gamma$ take $\bigotimes_{v} \mathcal P^\vee(g_v, n_v) \otimes \det E(\Gamma)$, where $\det E(\Gamma)$ is the top exterior power of the edge set. Isomorphisms of graphs permute the summands; take coinvariants. Stability makes this a finite sum.

steps.slogan: Give the sum the internal differential of $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: The differential of $\mathcal P$ acts on each vertex label, and the Leibniz rule with Koszul signs extends it to a differential $d_{\mathcal P}$ on every summand. It squares to zero because the differential of $\mathcal P$ does.

steps.slogan: Define the splitting differential by dualizing the composition of $\mathcal P$.
steps.detail: The dual of the composition at an edge maps a vertex label to a pair of labels at two vertices joined by a new edge. Summing over all vertices and all splittings, and wedging the new edge into $\det E$, gives $d_{\mathrm{split}}$ from the summand of $\Gamma$ to the summands of larger graphs.

steps.slogan: Show that $d^2 = 0$ by cancellation of signs.
steps.detail: The composition of $\mathcal P$ is a chain map, so $d_{\mathcal P}$ and $d_{\mathrm{split}}$ anticommute. Two splittings in either order give the same graph with the two new edges exchanged, which changes the sign in $\det E$, and associativity of the composition identifies the terms. So $d_{\mathrm{split}}^2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Define the modular operad structure by gluing graphs and check that it commutes with $d$.
steps.detail: Gluing two graphs along half-edges, or gluing two half-edges of one graph, gives a graph of the right type and joins the factors of $\det E$. These maps commute with $d$, so $F\mathcal P$ is a twisted modular operad with the dual twist.

steps.slogan: Restrict to genus $0$ and compare with the cobar construction.
steps.detail: A stable graph of genus $0$ has genus-$0$ vertices and no cycle, so it is a tree and $|E| = |V| - 1$. Trees with labels in $\mathcal P^\vee$ and the splitting differential form the [cobar construction](c:bar-construction) of the cyclic operad, and $\det E$ becomes a shift by the number of vertices.

concepts.c:modular-operad: The input is a modular operad, and the output is again one.
concepts.c:graph-complex: The sum over stable graphs with a differential is a graph complex.
concepts.c:bar-construction: In genus $0$ the construction is the cobar construction.

source.ref: E. Getzler and M. M. Kapranov, Modular operads, Compositio Mathematica 110 (1998), 65-126

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be irreducible closed [projective varieties](c:projective-variety) in [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb P^n$ over an algebraically closed field, with $\dim X + \dim Y > n$. Then $X \cap Y$ is nonempty and [connected](c:connected-space).

hypotheses.text: $X, Y \subseteq \mathbb P^n$ are irreducible closed [projective varieties](c:projective-variety) over an algebraically closed field.
The dimensions satisfy $\dim X + \dim Y > n$.

conclusion: The intersection $X \cap Y$ is nonempty and [connected](c:connected-space).

proofs.name: Join and diagonal subspace
proofs.slogan: Turn the diagonal into a linear subspace of $\mathbb P^{2n+1}$ by taking the join of $X$ and $Y$, then use connectedness of linear sections.
proofs.scope: The statement for two subvarieties, which is the form in the record; the cited paper proves it for morphisms from an irreducible complete variety to $\mathbb P^n \times \mathbb P^n$. The last step is the classical connectedness of linear sections.

roles.why: Irreducibility makes the join irreducible, which the connectedness of linear sections needs.
The inequality makes $\dim J$ exceed the codimension of the diagonal subspace.

steps.slogan: Place $X$ and $Y$ in disjoint copies of $\mathbb P^n$ inside $\mathbb P^{2n+1}$ and form their join $J$.
steps.detail: Let $L_1 = \{[x:0]\}$ and $L_2 = \{[0:y]\}$, and let $J$ be the join of $X \subseteq L_1$ and $Y \subseteq L_2$: the closure of the points $[x:y]$ with $x$ and $y$ in the affine cones over $X$ and $Y$. This is irreducible, being the closure of a $\mathbb G_m$-bundle over $X \times Y$, and $\dim J = \dim X + \dim Y + 1$.

steps.slogan: Identify $J \cap \Lambda$ with $X \cap Y$ for the diagonal subspace $\Lambda = \{[x:x]\}$.
steps.detail: The [linear subspace](c:linear-subspace) $\Lambda \cong \mathbb P^n$ has codimension $n+1$ and misses $L_1 \cup L_2$. A point $[x:x]$ lies in $J$ exactly when $x$ lies in both cones. So the isomorphism $\mathbb P^n \to \Lambda$ maps $X \cap Y$ onto $J \cap \Lambda$.

steps.slogan: Compare dimensions: $\dim J = \dim X + \dim Y + 1 > n + 1$.
steps.detail: The hypothesis gives $\dim J \ge n + 2$, which is larger than the codimension $n + 1$ of $\Lambda$. By the dimension theorem for projective varieties, $J \cap \Lambda$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Apply the connectedness of linear sections of an irreducible variety.
steps.detail: Let $W$ be the incidence variety of pairs $(z, L)$ with $z \in J \cap L$, over the Grassmannian of codimension-$(n+1)$ subspaces. It is irreducible, and by Bertini a general fibre is connected since $\dim J > n+1$. Zariski's connectedness theorem then makes every fibre connected, in particular $J \cap \Lambda \cong X \cap Y$.

concepts.c:projective-variety: The varieties $X$ and $Y$ and their join are projective, so linear sections behave well.
concepts.c:projective-space: The join lives in $\mathbb P^{2n+1}$, where the diagonal is linear.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of $X \cap Y$ is the conclusion.
concepts.c:linear-subspace: The diagonal becomes a linear subspace, so classical results apply.

source.ref: W. Fulton and J. Hansen, A connectedness theorem for projective varieties, with applications to intersections and singularities of mappings, Annals of Mathematics 110 (1979), 159-166
source.note: Proves the connectedness theorem for morphisms into the product of two projective spaces; the join construction replaces the diagonal by a linear subspace.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) with trivial [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle). Then the [differential graded Lie algebra](c:differential-graded-lie-algebra) $A^{0,*}(T_X)$ is quasi-abelian: a chain of [quasi-isomorphisms](c:quasi-isomorphism) of dg Lie algebras joins it to an [abelian dg Lie algebra](c:abelian-differential-graded-lie-algebra).

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold).
The [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) of $X$ is trivial: there is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic $n$-form $\Omega$, where $n = \dim X$.

conclusion: The Kodaira-Spencer dg Lie algebra $A^{0,*}(T_X)$ is connected by dg Lie algebra quasi-isomorphisms to an abelian dg Lie algebra.

proofs.name: BV operator and the dd-bar lemma
proofs.slogan: Transport the Dolbeault algebra to a BV algebra, restrict to the kernel of the BV operator, and use the dd-bar lemma for the quasi-isomorphisms.
proofs.scope: The hypotheses compact and Kähler are implicit in the source record; without them the dd-bar lemma may fail. Goldman and Millson proved the statement first, and the outline is the algebraic proof of Iacono and Manetti.

roles.why: Compactness and the Kähler metric give Hodge theory and hence the dd-bar lemma.
A nowhere vanishing holomorphic $n$-form turns polyvector fields into forms.

steps.slogan: Use $\Omega$ to turn polyvector fields into forms and get a BV operator $\Delta$.
steps.detail: Contraction with $\Omega$ gives isomorphisms $\wedge^p T_X \cong \Omega^{n-p}_X$, so $A^{0,*}(\wedge^* T_X) \cong A^{n-*,*}$. Transporting $\partial$ gives an operator $\Delta$ of order at most $2$ with $\Delta^2 = 0$ that anticommutes with $\bar\partial$.

steps.slogan: Express the Schouten bracket through $\Delta$ by the Tian-Todorov identity.
steps.detail: For polyvector fields, $[a,b] = \pm\bigl(\Delta(ab) - \Delta(a)\,b \mp a\,\Delta(b)\bigr)$. So on elements killed by $\Delta$ the bracket equals $\pm\Delta(ab)$, which lies in $\operatorname{im}\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Restrict to the sub-dgla $K = \ker\Delta$ and its abelian quotient $K/\operatorname{im}\Delta$.
steps.detail: Since $\Delta$ anticommutes with $\bar\partial$ and $\Delta^2 = 0$, $K$ is closed under $\bar\partial$ and the bracket and contains $\operatorname{im}\Delta$. The bracket of $K$ lies in $\operatorname{im}\Delta$, which is therefore a dg ideal with abelian quotient. In polyvector degree $1$ this gives dgla maps $A^{0,*}(T_X) \leftarrow K \to K/\operatorname{im}\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Show with the dd-bar lemma that both maps are [quasi-isomorphisms](c:quasi-isomorphism).
steps.detail: On a compact Kähler manifold Hodge theory gives the $\partial\bar\partial$-lemma. For the double complex $(A^{*,*}, \partial, \bar\partial)$ it makes $\ker\partial \hookrightarrow A^{*,*}$ and $\ker\partial \to \ker\partial/\operatorname{im}\partial$ quasi-isomorphisms for $\bar\partial$. Transported by $\Omega$, these are the inclusion $K \subseteq A^{0,*}(\wedge^*T_X)$ and the projection $K \to K/\operatorname{im}\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $A^{0,*}(T_X)$ is quasi-isomorphic to an abelian dg Lie algebra.
steps.detail: The zigzag of dgla quasi-isomorphisms $A^{0,*}(T_X) \leftarrow K \to K/\operatorname{im}\Delta$ ends in an abelian dgla, whose cohomology is $H^*(X, T_X)$. So the Kodaira-Spencer dgla is quasi-abelian.

concepts.c:kahler-manifold: The Kähler metric gives Hodge theory and the dd-bar lemma.
concepts.c:canonical-bundle: Triviality of the canonical bundle gives the form $\Omega$ and the BV operator.
concepts.c:differential-graded-lie-algebra: The Dolbeault complex of vector fields is the dg Lie algebra to be studied.
concepts.c:quasi-isomorphism: Quasi-isomorphisms are the maps in the chain that joins the algebras.
concepts.c:abelian-differential-graded-lie-algebr: The end of the chain is an abelian dg Lie algebra.

source.ref: D. Iacono and M. Manetti, An algebraic proof of Bogomolov-Tian-Todorov theorem, in Deformation Spaces, Aspects of Mathematics E40, Vieweg+Teubner 2010, 113-133; the statement is due to W.
